Wadawurrung ('Wathaurong') is in on the coast in green. | states = [[Australia]] | extinct = ? | revived = 1998{{Cite web |title=Vaclang.org.au |url=http://www.vaclang.org.au/languages/wathaurong-language-program-geelong.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221116005436/http://www.vaclang.org.au/languages/wathaurong-language-program-geelong.html |archive-date=16 November 2022 |access-date=2024-12-28 |website=www.vaclang.org.au |url-status=live }} }} '''Wadawurrung''', also rendered as '''Wathawurrung''', '''Wathaurong''' or '''Wada wurrung''', and formerly sometimes '''Barrabool''', is the [[Aboriginal Australian language]] spoken by the [[Wadawurrung people]] of the [[Kulin Nation|Kulin]] Nation of Central [[Victoria (Australia)|Victoria]]. It was spoken by 15 clans south of the [[Werribee River]] and the [[Bellarine Peninsula]] to [[Streatham, Victoria|Streatham]]. Various regional programs and initiatives promote the usage and revitalisation of Wadawurrung language. ==Phonology== === Consonants === Blake reconstructs Wadawurrung consonants as such:{{Cite web |last1=Blake |first1=Barry J. |last2=Clark |first2=Ian |last3=Krishna-Pillay |first3=Sharnthi H. |date=1998 |title=Wathawurrung and the Colac language of Southern Victoria |url=https://openresearch-repository.anu.edu.au/bitstream/1885/146194/1/PL-C147%20(1).pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201129233035/https://openresearch-repository.anu.edu.au/bitstream/1885/146194/1/PL-C147%20(1).pdf |url-status=live |archive-date=29 November 2020 }} {| class="wikitable" style="text-align: center" |+ ! ![[Labial consonant|Labial]] ![[Alveolar consonant|Alveolar]] ![[Laminal consonant|Laminal]] ![[Retroflex consonant|Retroflex]] ![[Velar consonant|Velar]] |- ![[Stop consonant|Stops]] |p/b {{IPAblink|p}} |t/d {{IPAblink|t}} |th/dh {{IPAblink|t̪}}
tj/dj {{IPAblink|c}} |rt/rd {{IPAblink|ʈ}} |k/g {{IPAblink|k}} |- ![[Nasal consonant|Nasals]] |m {{IPAblink|m}} |n {{IPAblink|n}} |nh/ny [{{IPA link|n̪}}, {{IPA link|ɲ}}] |rn {{IPAblink|ɳ}} |ng {{IPAblink|ŋ}} |- ![[Lateral consonant|Laterals]] | |l {{IPAblink|l}} |ly {{IPAblink|ʎ̟}} |rl {{IPAblink|ɭ}} | |- ![[Rhotic consonant|Rhotics]] | |rr [{{IPA link|ɾ}} / {{IPA link|r}}] | |r {{IPAblink|ɽ}} | |- ![[Glide consonant|Glides]] | | |y {{IPAblink|j}} | |w {{IPAblink|w}} |} Due to the varied nature of attestations of the language, Blake reconstructs Wadawurrung consonants in complacence to the standard features of [[Australian Aboriginal languages|the Australian Languages]]. It is presumed that Wadawurrung did not distinguish between voiced and unvoiced consonants ('Parrwong ~ Barwon' – [[Australian magpie|Magpie]]). What Blake attributes as a distinction between 'alveolar' and 'laminal' consonants is better described as a distinction between dental and post-alveolar pronunciation on nasal and stop consonants. This is a distinction in indigenous language families of the Australian south-east such as [[Yuin–Kuric languages|Yuin-Kuric]] (incl. [[Ngunnawal language|Ngunnawal]] and [[Dharug language|Dharug]]) and the [[Gippsland languages]] (Incl. [[Dhudhuroa language|Dhudhuroa]]). It is presumed there was no distinction between post-alveolar {{IPA|/n/}} and palatal {{IPA|/ɲ/}} ('Nhita' – to steal, fluctuates with 'nyita'). It is assumed that a similar correspondence occurs with the post-alveolar stop, thus mixed attestation between ''''th'''', ''''tj'''' & ''''ty''''. The post-alveolar consonants {{IPA|/ʎ̟/, /t/ and /ɲ/}} in word final position are rendered as ''''yl'''', ''''yt'''' & ''''yn'''', respectively. E.g. 'Gowa'''yn'''' – [[Eel]]. The word final nasal after /a/ is always cited as ''''ayn'''' due to its fluctuation with 'ng' in sources Blake asserts that sources do not differentiate between alveolar {{IPA|/r/}} and retroflex {{IPA|/ɽ/}} and the distinction is thus presumed from comparison to other Victorian Aboriginal Languages. Blake represents every rhotic as 'rr' unless drawing from modern sources such as [[Luise Hercus|Hercus]]. === Vowels === Blake does not specify the number of vowels present in Wadawurrung. The standard set of {{IPA|/a/, /e/, /i/, /o/}} and {{IPA|/u/}} are used, however Blake notes a consistent correspondence between ''''a'''', ''''u'''' and ''''o'''' in various sources ('Djinang' – foot, variously attested as 'jinnung', 'genong'). There is also fluctuation between ''''a'''' and ''''e'''' as the last vowel in a word ('walart' – possum, compared to 'wollert'), however Blake maintains that they are distinct vowels == Vocabulary == === Place names === Select placenames with attested origin in Wathawurrung language terms are: {| class="wikitable sortable" |- !
